events.title: Coastal Flood Advisory
events.description: * WHAT...Up to 1.7 ft of inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. * WHERE...Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay. * WHEN...From 5 PM Friday to 2 AM PDT Thursday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to be 1.0 ft above normal (6.84 ft MLLW) at 6:55 PM Friday 8/7, 1.3 ft above normal (7.15 ft MLLW) at 8:00 PM Saturday 8/8, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 9:02 PM Sunday 8/9, 1.7 ft above normal (7.56 ft MLLW) at 10:01 PM Monday 8/10, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 10:57 PM Tuesday 8/11, and 1.3 ft above normal (7.14 ft MLLW) at 11:49 PM Wednesday 8/12. These predictions include both astronomical tides and roughly 3-6 inches of additional water mainly from a combination of thermal expansion and accumulated sea level rise since the tidal datum was established (1983-2001). High tide varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.

location.region: San Francisco; North Bay Interior Valleys; San Francisco Bay Shoreline; Northern Monterey Bay; Southern Monterey Bay and Big Sur Coast

weather.headline: Coastal Flood Advisory issued August 6 at 7:45PM PDT until August 13 at 2:00AM PDT by NWS San Francisco CA
weather.description:
* WHAT...Up to 1.7 ft of inundation above ground level is
possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways.

* WHERE...Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San
Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay.

* WHEN...From 5 PM Friday to 2 AM PDT Thursday.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only
isolated road closures expected.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide
is expected to be 1.0 ft above normal (6.84 ft MLLW) at 6:55 PM
Friday 8/7, 1.3 ft above normal (7.15 ft MLLW) at 8:00 PM
Saturday 8/8, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 9:02 PM
Sunday 8/9, 1.7 ft above normal (7.56 ft MLLW) at 10:01 PM
Monday 8/10, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 10:57 PM
Tuesday 8/11, and 1.3 ft above normal (7.14 ft MLLW) at 11:49 PM
Wednesday 8/12. These predictions include both astronomical
tides and roughly 3-6 inches of additional water mainly from a
combination of thermal expansion and accumulated sea level rise
since the tidal datum was established (1983-2001). High tide
varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast
and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.
weather.instruction:
High tides may result in flooding along coastal trails, cut off
access to some low-lying beaches and coastal areas, and bring
water and waves farther up the beach than typical. If travel is
required, allow extra time as some roads may be closed. Do not
drive, bike, or walk around barricades or through water of
unknown depth. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone
property.

events.title: Extreme Heat Warning
events.description: * WHAT...High temperatures 100 to 105 degrees in the valleys each afternoon. Low temperatures 73 to 78 degrees in the valleys each night. This will result in a major risk for heat-related illnesses for much of the population, especially those without effective cooling. * WHERE...Southeastern Elko County. * WHEN...Until 11 PM PDT Monday. * IMPACTS...Heat-related illnesses increase significantly during extreme heat events.

location.region: Southeastern Elko County

weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued August 7 at 10:54AM PDT until August 10 at 11:00PM PDT by NWS Elko NV
weather.description:
* WHAT...High temperatures 100 to 105 degrees in the valleys each
afternoon. Low temperatures 73 to 78 degrees in the valleys each
night. This will result in a major risk for heat-related illnesses
for much of the population, especially those without effective
cooling.

* WHERE...Southeastern Elko County.

* WHEN...Until 11 PM PDT Monday.

* IMPACTS...Heat-related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events.
weather.instruction:
Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Drink plenty of fluids, remain in an air-conditioned room, stay out
of the sun, and check on relatives and neighbors.
weather.areaDesc: Southeastern Elko County

events.title: Coastal Flood Advisory
events.description: * WHAT...Up to 1.6 ft of inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. * WHERE...Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay. * WHEN...From 5 PM Friday to 2 AM PDT Thursday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to be 1.0 ft above normal (6.84 ft MLLW) at 6:55 PM Friday 8/7, 1.4 ft above normal (7.25 ft MLLW) at 8:00 PM Saturday 8/8, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 9:02 PM Sunday 8/9, 1.6 ft above normal (7.46 ft MLLW) at 10:01 PM Monday 8/10, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 10:57 PM Tuesday 8/11, and 1.3 ft above normal (7.14 ft MLLW) at 11:49 PM Wednesday 8/12. These predictions include both astronomical tides and roughly 3-6 inches of additional water mainly from a combination of thermal expansion and accumulated sea level rise since the tidal datum was established (1983-2001). High tide varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.

events.description: * WHAT...Large breaking waves of 9 to 11 feet and dangerous rip currents expected. * WHERE...Along west and north facing reefs. * WHEN...Until 4 PM ChST Thursday. * IMPACTS...Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions and localized beach erosion. Rip currents can sweep even the best swimmers away from shore into deeper water. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...A strong monsoon pattern continues to produce hazardous surf and a high risk of rip currents along west and north-facing reefs. As influence from Typhoon Dolphin on the monsoon pattern decreases, influence from Tropical Storm Chan-Hom and other disturbances will increase. This will keep surf elevated and above hazardous conditions for west and north facing reefs through much of the coming week, and surf hazards have been extended through Thursday afternoon. The High Surf Advisory and High Rip Current Risk may be extended again next week as the monsoon pattern, and associated west to northwest swells, continue.

events.title: Iran warned Gulf states it would hit their energy infrastructure if the US struck again, and the hosts then lobbied Washington to hold off
events.description: Iran cannot win a fight for the airspace over the Gulf. It can raise the cost for the states whose runways the US flies from, and let them carry the argument into Washington. Trump cancelled planned strikes on Iran on 1 August. On Air Force One the following day he named the governments that had asked him to hold off, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Iran, and he called the cancelled operation "the biggest attack since World War II" (AP, 2 August). On his account, the target asked to be spared alongside the hosts. Tehran denies making any request, and of the four, only the Saudi call is independently sourced. Reuters reported on 5 August, citing five sources, what had moved the phone calls. Iran had warned Gulf states that any new US attack on its territory would trigger retaliation against critical energy infrastructure across the region. An Iranian official's list ran to energy facilities, refineries, electricity grids, water infrastructure, transport networks and oil fields. Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi carried the message himself to his Saudi, Turkish and Qatari counterparts and to Pakistan's army chief. There is a bill attached to hosting the runways. On 28 July US Central Command and the Saudi Armed Forces jointly struck Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces, an umbrella of Iran-aligned paramilitaries formally integrated into the Iraqi state, across seven provinces; at least 20 PMF members were killed and 32 wounded, on the PMF's own count (CENTCOM, 28 July; BBC and Al Jazeera, 29 July). The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, a coalition of Iranian-backed Iraqi militias, set a response deadline of after 6 August, conditioned on Saudi Arabia meeting demands that include an official apology (Critical Threats Project / Institute for the Study of War, 6 August). The strike was joint. The apology is demanded of Riyadh alone. Riyadh is building its own insurance in the meantime. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on the morning of 7 August, under which an armed attack on any one of the three counts as an attack on all three (Reuters, 7 August). The cheapest deterrent in the region costs Iran nothing to maintain. I write the Fault Line Extra. Today's issue is free to read, every claim sourced: https://fault-line.io/extra-010/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_content=foreignpolicy-extra010&utm_campaign=extra submitted by /u/Mikeynphoto2009 to r/foreignpolicy [link] [comments]

weather.instruction:
Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Drink plenty of fluids, remain in an air-conditioned room, stay out
of the sun, and check on relatives and neighbors.

events.title: Coastal Flood Advisory
events.description: * WHAT...Up to 1.6 ft of inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. * WHERE...Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay. * WHEN...Until 2 AM PDT Thursday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to be 1.4 ft above normal (7.25 ft MLLW) at 8:00 PM Saturday 8/8, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 9:02 PM Sunday 8/9, 1.6 ft above normal (7.46 ft MLLW) at 10:01 PM Monday 8/10, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 10:57 PM Tuesday 8/11, and 1.3 ft above normal (7.14 ft MLLW) at 11:49 PM Wednesday 8/12. These predictions include both astronomical tides and roughly 3-6 inches of additional water mainly from a combination of thermal expansion and accumulated sea level rise since the tidal datum was established (1983-2001). High tide varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.

events.title: Rip Current Statement
events.description: * WHAT...Large breaking waves of 9 to 11 feet and dangerous rip currents expected. * WHERE...Along west and north facing reefs. * WHEN...Until 4 PM ChST Thursday. * IMPACTS...Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions and localized beach erosion. Rip currents can sweep even the best swimmers away from shore into deeper water. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...A strong monsoon pattern continues to produce hazardous surf and a high risk of rip currents along west and north-facing reefs. As influence from Typhoon Dolphin on the monsoon pattern decreases, influence from Tropical Storm Chan-Hom and other disturbances will increase. This will keep surf elevated and above hazardous conditions for west and north facing reefs through much of the coming week, and surf hazards have been extended through Thursday afternoon. The High Surf Advisory and High Rip Current Risk may be extended again next week as the monsoon pattern, and associated west to northwest swells, continue.

the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

heat stroke.

seek out resources provided by your local community management.

events.title: Coastal Flood Advisory
events.description: * WHAT...Up to 1.7 ft of inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. * WHERE...Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay. * WHEN...Until 2 AM PDT Thursday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to be 1.4 ft above normal (7.25 ft MLLW) at 8:00 PM Saturday 8/8, 1.7 ft above normal (7.54 ft MLLW) at 9:02 PM Sunday 8/9, 1.7 ft above normal (7.56 ft MLLW) at 10:01 PM Monday 8/10, 1.7 ft above normal (7.54 ft MLLW) at 10:57 PM Tuesday 8/11, and 1.4 ft above normal (7.24 ft MLLW) at 11:49 PM Wednesday 8/12. These predictions include both astronomical tides and roughly 4-8 inches of additional water mainly from a combination of thermal expansion and accumulated sea level rise since the tidal datum was established (1983- 2001). High tide varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.

location.region: San Francisco; North Bay Interior Valleys; San Francisco Bay Shoreline; Northern Monterey Bay; Southern Monterey Bay and Big Sur Coast

weather.instruction:
Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

of the sun, and check on relatives and neighbors.

* WHERE...Indian Wells Valley, Mojave Desert, and Mojave Desert
Slopes.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events, especially those with little overnight relief
from the heat.

temperatures up to 112 degrees. Overnight lows will range from
75-80 degrees.
weather.instruction:

the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

Stay cool, stay hydrated, stay informed.

If you do not have air conditioning in your home or lack shelter,
seek out resources provided by your local community management.

weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued August 8 at 9:42PM PDT until August 10 at 11:00PM PDT by NWS Elko NV
weather.description:
* WHAT...High temperatures 100 to 105 degrees in the valleys each
afternoon. Low temperatures 73 to 78 degrees in the valleys each
night. This will result in a major risk for heat-related illnesses
for much of the population, especially those without effective
cooling.

* WHERE...Southeastern Elko County.

* WHEN...Until 11 PM PDT Monday.

* IMPACTS...Heat-related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events.
weather.instruction:
Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Drink plenty of fluids, remain in an air-conditioned room, stay out
of the sun, and check on relatives and neighbors.

events.title: Coastal Flood Advisory
events.description: * WHAT...Up to 1.6 ft of inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. * WHERE...Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay. * WHEN...Until 2 AM PDT Thursday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to be 1.5 ft above normal (7.34 ft MLLW) at 9:02 PM Sunday 8/9, 1.5 ft above normal (7.36 ft MLLW) at 10:01 PM Monday 8/10, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 10:57 PM Tuesday 8/11, and 1.3 ft above normal (7.14 ft MLLW) at 11:49 PM Wednesday 8/12. These predictions include both astronomical tides and roughly 3-6 inches of additional water mainly from a combination of thermal expansion and accumulated sea level rise since the tidal datum was established (1983- 2001). High tide varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.

location.region: San Francisco; North Bay Interior Valleys; San Francisco Bay Shoreline; Northern Monterey Bay; Southern Monterey Bay and Big Sur Coast

weather.instruction:
A Heat Advisory is issued when the combination of heat and humidity
is expected to make it feel like it is 95 to 99 degrees for two or
more consecutive days, or 100 to 104 degrees for any length of time.

Seniors and those with chronic health problems or mental health
conditions are at an increased risk. Homes without air conditioning
can be much hotter than outdoor temperatures.

Use air conditioning to stay cool at home or go to a place that has
air conditioning. If you don't have home air conditioning, continue
to seek out cool spaces each day as long as it remains hot, and for a
few days after if your home is still hot. Check on vulnerable
friends, family members and neighbors.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an

more consecutive days, or 100 to 104 degrees for any length of time.

Seniors and those with chronic health problems or mental health
conditions are at an increased risk. Homes without air conditioning
can be much hotter than outdoor temperatures.

Use air conditioning to stay cool at home or go to a place that has
air conditioning. If you don't have home air conditioning, continue
to seek out cool spaces each day as long as it remains hot, and for a
few days after if your home is still hot. Check on vulnerable
friends, family members and neighbors.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! In cases of heat stroke call 9 1 1.

don't get too tight and be aware of overwash around boat ramps at
high tide. Any recreational watercraft on beaches, such as canoes,
should be secured or moved.

even by local standards, will occur. Actions should be taken to
lessen the impact of the extreme heat.

evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat

weather.description:
* WHAT...Heat index values around 95.

* WHERE...Southern Fairfield and Southern New Haven Counties.

* WHEN...Until 7 PM EDT Monday.

* IMPACTS...Hot temperatures and high humidity may cause heat
illnesses.
weather.instruction:
A Heat Advisory is issued when the combination of heat and humidity
is expected to make it feel like it is 95 to 99 degrees for two or
more consecutive days, or 100 to 104 degrees for any length of time.

Seniors and those with chronic health problems or mental health
conditions are at an increased risk. Homes without air conditioning
can be much hotter than outdoor temperatures.

Use air conditioning to stay cool at home or go to a place that has
air conditioning. If you don't have home air conditioning, continue
to seek out cool spaces each day as long as it remains hot, and for a
few days after if your home is still hot. Check on vulnerable
friends, family members and neighbors.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! In cases of heat stroke call 9 1 1.
weather.areaDesc: Southern Fairfield; Southern New Haven

weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued August 9 at 3:08PM CDT until August 12 at 8:00PM CDT by NWS Springfield MO
weather.description:
* WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions with heat index values up to 108.

* WHERE...Portions of southeast Kansas and central, southwest, and
west central Missouri.

* WHEN...Until 8 PM CDT Wednesday.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat and high humidity events.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

events.title: Coastal Flood Statement
events.description: ...MINOR COASTAL FLOODING DURING HIGH TIDE THROUGH MID WEEK... .Peak monthly high tides combined with water levels that are running higher than predicted will lead to minor flooding in low- lying coastal areas. Coastal flooding is possible through at least Tuesday around the daily peak tide, which will be during the afternoon hours. By Wednesday, tides are forecast to decrease, though coastal flooding may still be possible for select locations where water levels are running highest. * WHAT...Isolated minor coastal flooding expected. * WHERE...Vulnerable low-lying coastal roadways, docks, boat ramps and other coastal infrastructure. * WHEN...The afternoon hours today through Tuesday, at and around daily peak tides. * IMPACTS...Flooding of beaches that are normally dry, minor coastal erosion, and saltwater inundation of low-lying roads, docks, boat ramps and other coastal infrastructure.

weather.description:
...MINOR COASTAL FLOODING DURING HIGH TIDE THROUGH MID WEEK...

.Peak monthly high tides combined with water levels that are
running higher than predicted will lead to minor flooding in low-
lying coastal areas. Coastal flooding is possible through at
least Tuesday around the daily peak tide, which will be during
the afternoon hours. By Wednesday, tides are forecast to
decrease, though coastal flooding may still be possible for
select locations where water levels are running highest.

* WHAT...Isolated minor coastal flooding expected.

* WHERE...Vulnerable low-lying coastal roadways, docks, boat
ramps and other coastal infrastructure.

* WHEN...The afternoon hours today through Tuesday, at and
around daily peak tides.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of beaches that are normally dry, minor
coastal erosion, and saltwater inundation of low-lying roads,
docks, boat ramps and other coastal infrastructure.
weather.instruction:
Avoid driving through flooded roadways. If you are forced to
drive through salt water, be sure to rinse your vehicle with
fresh water. Move electronics, vehicles or other valuables to
higher ground. Monitor vessels to ensure mooring lines don't get
too tight and watch out for overwash around boat ramps. Secure
canoes or other watercraft stowed on beaches.

weather.description:
* WHAT...Very warm afternoon temperatures in the middle to upper
70s, with overnight temperatures in the low to mid 50s.

* WHERE...Lower Matanuska Valley.

* WHEN...Until 8 PM AKDT Monday.

* IMPACTS...Individuals not accustomed to these unusually warm
temperatures for this region may experience heat related illnesses.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids and check up on elderly and vulnerable
relatives and neighbors.

Take extra precautions when working in the sun. Wear sunscreen and
lightweight, loose fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous
activities to early morning or evening. Take action when you see
symptoms of heat exhaustion.

Close curtains during the daytime to reduce sun insolation into the
home and open windows at night to allow the home to cool off.
Utilize fans or community buildings with air conditioning.

weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat

criteria.

Weather Service and area fire management agencies.

weather.instruction:
Air pollutants can cause breathing difficulties for children, the
elderly, as well as persons with respiratory problems. Those
individuals who are sensitive to increased particulate matter or
smoke are encouraged to avoid prolonged or strenuous outdoor
activity during this advisory. Open burning is prohibited by air
quality rule. It is also recommended that all other individuals
limit prolonged or strenuous activity outdoors.

THIS STATEMENT IS ISSUED BY THE IDAHO DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL
QUALITY, AIR QUALITY GROUP. FOR MORE INFORMATION, CONTACT DEQ's
Idaho Falls Regional Office at (208)528-2650.

events.title: Air Quality Alert
events.description: Oregon Department of Environmental Quality has issued an Air Quality Advisory...in effect until noon PDT Monday for eastern Douglas County...mainly for areas in the south Umpqua River valley near Tiller and the Umpqua National Forest east of Steamboat. Wildfires burning in the region combined with forecast conditions will cause air quality levels to fluctuate and could be at unhealthy levels at times. Smoke levels can change rapidly depending on the weather. People at risk include infants and young children, people with heart or lung disease, older adults and pregnant people. People can take the following precautions to protect their health: * Follow local burn restrictions to prevent deteriorating air quality. * Avoid strenuous outdoor activity during periods of poor air quality. * People with heart or lung problems and young children are especially vulnerable. These people should stay indoors while smoke levels are high. * Use certified High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filters in indoor heating, ventilation, cooling and air purification systems. For additional information...please visit the web site at https://oregonsmoke.org

events.title: Air Quality Alert
events.description: The following message is transmitted on behalf of the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality, Air Quality Division and the Wyoming Department of Health. WHAT...Air Quality Alert for Wildfire Smoke. WHERE...Sheridan County, Wyoming. WHEN...Through noon Monday. IMPACTS...Heavy smoke from regional wildfires will continue to reduce air quality. HEALTH INFORMATION...The Wyoming Department of Health recommends the elderly, young children, and individuals with respiratory problems avoid excessive physical exertion and minimize outdoor activities during this time. Wildfire smoke is made up of a variety of pollutants, including particulate matter and ozone, which can cause respiratory health effects. Although these people are most susceptible to health impacts, the Department of Health also advises that everyone should avoid prolonged exposure to poor air quality conditions. CURRENT CONDITIONS...The Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality, Air Quality Division offers near real-time air quality data for Wyoming's monitoring stations and health effects information to help the public interpret current conditions. Current air quality conditions across the state of Wyoming can be found at http://www.wyvisnet.com/

events.description: The following message is transmitted on behalf of the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality, Air Quality Division, and the Wyoming Department of Health. * WHAT...Air Quality Alert for Wildfire Smoke. * WHERE...All of Western and Central Wyoming * WHEN...Now through Noon Monday. * IMPACTS...Smoke from western United States wildfires continues to be observed across much of western and central Wyoming. The smoke is limiting visibilities at times. HEALTH INFORMATION...The Wyoming Department of Health recommends that the elderly, young children, and individuals with respiratory problems avoid excessive physical exertion and minimize outdoor activities during this time. Wildfire smoke is made up of a variety of pollutants, including particulate matter and ozone, which can cause respiratory health effects. Although these people are most susceptible to health impacts, the Department of Health also advises that everyone should avoid prolonged exposure to poor air quality conditions. CURRENT CONDITIONS...The Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality, Air Quality Division offers near real-time air quality data for Wyoming's monitoring stations and health effects information to help the public interpret current conditions. Current air quality conditions across the state of Wyoming can be found at http://www.wyvisnet.com/.

events.description: An Air Quality Alert has been issued by the following agencies: Washington Department of Ecology Colville Confederated Tribes Environmental Protection Agency Spokane Regional Clean Air Agency An Air Quality Alert has been issued for Adams, Asotin, Chelan, Douglas, Ferry, Garfield, Grant, Lincoln, Okanogan, Pend Oreille, Spokane, Stevens, and Whitman Counties until further notice due to current and expected smoke from regional fires. Critical fire weather this weekend will produce significant smoke from ongoing and emerging fires. Particulate matter (PM2.5) may reach Very Unhealthy levels for areas directly downwind from active wildfires. Other areas may reach Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups or worse. Intermittent clearing may occur due to windy conditions, but smoke production continues to be significant. When air quality is Unhealthy, everyone should reduce exposure. Limit time outside, avoid strenuous outdoor activity, and follow tips for cleaner indoor air. When air quality is Very Unhealthy, everyone should reduce exposure. Stay inside and filter indoor air to keep it cleaner. Go elsewhere for cleaner air, if needed.

events.title: Special Weather Statement
events.description: Unusually warm temperatures are likely through Monday early evening. The warmest temperatures will occur during the afternoon into early evening, today and Monday. High temperatures across the Anchorage Bowl and lower Hillside will be in the low to mid 70s. Expect warmer temperatures inland with cooler temperatures along the coast. The overnight low will be in the 50s. Take extra precautions when working in the sun. Wear sunscreen and lightweight, loose fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion. Close curtains during the daytime to reduce sun insolation into the home and open windows at night to allow the home to cool off. Utilize fans or community buildings with air conditioning. Metzler

weather.instruction:
A Heat Advisory is issued when the combination of heat and humidity
is expected to make it feel like it is 95 to 99 degrees for two or
more consecutive days, or 100 to 104 degrees for any length of time.

Seniors and those with chronic health problems or mental health
conditions are at an increased risk. Homes without air conditioning
can be much hotter than outdoor temperatures.

Use air conditioning to stay cool at home or go to a place that has
air conditioning. If you don't have home air conditioning, continue
to seek out cool spaces each day as long as it remains hot, and for a
few days after if your home is still hot. Check on vulnerable
friends, family members and neighbors.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! In cases of heat stroke call 9 1 1.

weather.instruction:
An Extreme Heat Warning means that a period of very hot temperatures,
even by local standards, will occur. Actions should be taken to
lessen the impact of the extreme heat.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible, reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting clothing when possible and
drink plenty of water.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Public cooling shelters are available in some areas. Consult county
officials for more details.

drainage areas is imminent or may already be occurring. Persons in
the advisory area should use caution and avoid flood waters.

dangers of flooding.

Rip currents can sweep even the best swimmers away from shore into deeper water. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...A strong monsoon pattern continues to produce hazardous surf and a high risk of rip currents along west and north facing reefs through Thursday afternoon. The High Surf Advisory and High Rip Current Risk may be extended again as the monsoon pattern, and associated west to northwest swells, continue into next week.

events.title: Coastal Flood Advisory
events.description: * WHAT...Up to 1.6 ft of inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. * WHERE...Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, and Monterey Bay. * WHEN...Until 2 AM PDT Thursday. * IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only isolated road closures expected. * ADDITIONAL DETAILS...At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide is expected to be 1.6 ft above normal (7.46 ft MLLW) at 10:01 PM Monday 8/10, 1.6 ft above normal (7.44 ft MLLW) at 10:57 PM Tuesday 8/11, and 1.4 ft above normal (7.24 ft MLLW) at 11:49 PM Wednesday 8/12. These predictions include both astronomical tides and roughly 3-6 inches of additional water mainly from a combination of thermal expansion and accumulated sea level rise since the tidal datum was established (1983-2001). High tide varies up to 90 minutes earlier or later along the Pacific Coast and through the San Francisco Bay, respectively.

events.title: Air Quality Alert
events.description: AQAMT The Montana Department of Environmental Quality has issued an air quality alert for Beaverhead, Broadwater, Deer Lodge, Flathead, Gallatin, Granite, Jefferson, Lake, Lewis and Clark, Lincoln, Madison, Mineral, Missoula, Park, Powell, Ravalli, Silver Bow, Sweet Grass, Sanders, Yellowstone counties in effect until 9AM on 08/11/2026 An Air Quality Alert means that particulates have been trending upwards and that an exceedance of the 24 hour National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) has occurred or may occur in the near future. Elevated particulate levels from wildfire smoke As of 7AM on 08/10/2026, particulate levels in Columbia Falls, Frenchtown, Libby and Missoula are Unhealthy. As of 7AM on 08/10/2026, particulate levels in Billings, Dillon, Great Falls, Helena and Thompson Falls are Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups. As of 7AM on 08/10/2026, particulate levels in Butte, Cut Bank, Hamilton, Lewistown and Sleeping Giant are Moderate. When air quality is Unhealthy... State and local health officials recommend that people with respiratory or heart disease, the elderly, and children should avoid prolonged exertion; everyone else should limit prolonged exertion. When air quality is Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups... State and local health officials recommend that people with respiratory or heart disease, the elderly and children should limit prolonged exertion. When air quality is Moderate... State and local health officials recommend that unusually sensitive people should consider reducing prolonged or heavy exertion. For more information visit the Montana Department of Environmental Quality at http://todaysair.mtdeq.us

events.title: Coastal Flood Statement
events.description: ...MINOR COASTAL FLOODING DURING HIGH TIDE THROUGH MID WEEK... .Peak monthly high tides combined with water levels that are running higher than predicted will lead to minor flooding in low- lying coastal areas. Coastal flooding is possible through at least Tuesday around the daily peak tide, which will be during the afternoon hours. By Wednesday, tides are forecast to decrease, though coastal flooding may still be possible for select locations where water levels are running highest. * WHAT...Isolated minor coastal flooding. * WHERE...Vulnerable low-lying coastal roadways, docks, boat ramps and other coastal infrastructure. * WHEN...The afternoon hours through Tuesday, at and around daily peak tides. * IMPACTS...Flooding of beaches that are normally dry, minor coastal erosion, and saltwater inundation of low-lying roads, docks, boat ramps and other coastal infrastructure.

events.title: Extreme Heat Warning
events.description: * WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions with Major to Extreme Heat Risk. Highs 106 to 112 degrees. * WHERE...San Joaquin Valley and adjacent foothills, Lake Isabella, and the Kern River Valley. * WHEN...Until 8 PM PDT this evening. * IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during extreme heat events, especially those with little overnight relief from the heat.

location.region: Indian Wells Valley; Mojave Desert Slopes; Mojave Desert

weather.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued August 10 at 3:51AM PDT until August 10 at 8:00PM PDT by NWS Hanford CA
weather.description:
* WHAT...Dangerously hot conditions with Major to Extreme Heat Risk.
Highs 106 to 112 degrees.

* WHERE...San Joaquin Valley and adjacent foothills, Lake Isabella,
and the Kern River Valley.

* WHEN...Until 8 PM PDT this evening.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events, especially those with little overnight relief
from the heat.
weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

Stay cool, stay hydrated, stay informed.

If you do not have air conditioning in your home or lack shelter,
seek out resources provided by your local community management.
weather.areaDesc: Indian Wells Valley; Mojave Desert Slopes; Mojave Desert

weather.instruction:

shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Monitor the latest forecasts and warnings for updates.

weather.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Monitor the latest forecasts and warnings for updates.
